factories.name: Porto Manufacturing Co.
factories.story: A second-generation, family-run cut-and-sew workshop on the northern edge of Porto. Three floors: cutting, sewing, and finishing. The founder's daughter now runs production; many of the sewing team have been here for more than fifteen years.

process.detail: Fabric is relaxed for 24 hours before being cut on an automated table to minimise waste.
Teams of eight work in modular cells; each garment passes through 11 operations.
Every piece is steamed, measured against spec, and hand-inspected.
Recycled paper sleeves. No single-use plastic polybags.

factories.wages: Average wage 34% above the regional minimum

history.event: Founded as a four-person knitting workshop.

factories.name: Ege Denim Works
factories.story: A vertically integrated denim and bottoms factory near the Aegean coast, a short drive from the cotton fields that supply it. Water from laundry is treated and 60% recirculated on site.

process.detail: Rope-dyed yarn is woven on shuttle-less looms.
Computer-nested markers reduce cutting waste to under 12%.
Chain-stitched hems and bar-tacked stress points.
Ozone and laser finishing replace most stone washing.

factories.wages: Average wage 28% above the regional minimum

history.event: Opened in-house laundry with closed-loop water system.

factories.name: Saigon Outerwear Co.
factories.story: A technical outerwear specialist with seam-taping and down-filling lines. The factory runs an on-site clinic and a subsidised canteen for all workers.

process.detail: Laser cutting for technical fabrics to seal edges cleanly.
Specialist lines for canvas, quilting and taped seams.
Recycled insulation is weighed per panel for consistent warmth.
Seam strength and zipper cycle testing on every batch.

factories.wages: Average wage 41% above the regional minimum

history.event: Added seam-taping line for technical outerwear.

factories.name: Lanificio Alta Biella
factories.story: A knitwear house in the foothills of the Alps, where the soft local water has been used to finish wool for centuries. Garments are fully-fashioned — knitted to shape — so there is almost no cutting waste.

process.detail: Fully-fashioned panels knitted to shape on 12-gauge machines.
Panels are joined stitch by stitch by hand.
Washed in soft Alpine water to bloom the fibre.
Hand-pressed and measured before packing.

history.event: Founded as a family spinning mill.

factories.name: Kutch Shirting Co.
factories.story: A shirting specialist in Gujarat's textile district. Collars and cuffs are still turned and pressed by hand; the factory funds a worker-run savings cooperative.

process.detail: Stripes and checks are matched by hand at the cutting table.
Single-needle stitching at 18 stitches per inch.
Collars turned and pressed by hand for a clean point.
Mother-of-pearl-free, corozo nut buttons sewn with a shank.

factories.wages: Average wage 37% above the regional minimum

history.event: Moved to purpose-built facility with daylight floors.

factories.name: Vernon Cut & Sew
factories.story: A small, highly skilled fleece and loungewear workshop in Los Angeles. Every sewer is paid hourly, never by the piece.

process.detail: Fleece is cut in small lays to keep grain lines true.
Flatlock seams for comfort against the skin.
Selected colours are garment dyed for depth.
Every piece is measured and checked for pilling.

factories.wages: Hourly pay, 45% above the LA County minimum

history.event: Founded by two former pattern makers.
Moved to a larger space in Vernon.

journal.title: Why we publish our costs
journal.excerpt: Every product page shows what it costs to make. Here's how we calculate it — and what's left out.
body: Most clothing is priced by working backwards from what a shop thinks it can charge. We work forwards: materials, labour, transport and operations, then a brand margin we're willing to show you.
The breakdown on each product page is an estimate at the batch level. Material prices move; exchange rates move. We update the figures whenever we produce a new batch.
What's not in the number: marketing campaigns we don't run, wholesale markups we don't pay, and discounts we don't plan for. We don't run sales, so the price you see is the price everyone pays.
THREAD is a fictional brand. The figures on this site are simulated to illustrate the model.

journal.title: A day in Porto
journal.excerpt: Three floors, eleven operations, one tee. We spent a day at the workshop that makes our jersey.
body: At 7:30 the cutting floor is already warm. Fabric delivered yesterday has been left to relax overnight so it won't shrink after it's cut.
Upstairs, eight-person cells work through the eleven operations that turn flat panels into a finished tee. Nobody is paid by the piece — the pace is steady rather than frantic.
By late afternoon the finishing team is steaming and measuring. Anything more than half a centimetre out of spec goes back.

journal.title: The case for fewer, better pieces
journal.excerpt: The most sustainable garment is the one you already own. The second most is the one you'll wear for ten years.
body: We make a small number of things and try to make them very well. That means heavier fabrics, stronger seams, and fits that don't chase trends.
Cost per wear is a better measure than price. A $48 tee worn 200 times costs 24 cents a wear.
Every garment comes with a digital passport so you — or its next owner — can see where it came from and how to care for it.
